title: Testicular Cancer
subject: Pathology
summary: Testicular cancer is a germ‑cell malignancy of the testes, most often presenting as a painless scrotal mass. Early recognition, appropriate staging and timely surgery with adjuvant therapy give excellent cure rates, even in low‑resource settings.
aka: Germ cell tumor of the testis

sections.p: A malignant proliferation of germ cells arising in the testis, usually presenting as a unilateral, painless enlargement. Diagnosis requires a focused history, physical exam and scrotal ultrasound; tumor markers guide classification.
b: Painless testicular mass in a man >15 y
Ultrasound shows solid hypoechoic lesion
Serum AFP, β‑hCG, LDH for histologic clues

sections.p: Staging follows the AJCC TNM system (clinical stage I‑IV) and guides need for adjuvant therapy. In low‑resource hospitals, clinical stage (based on exam and limited imaging) often dictates management.
b: T1‑T4: size, invasion of tunica albuginea, epididymis, spermatic cord
N0‑N1: retroperitoneal lymph node size <2 cm vs ≥2 cm
M0‑M1: distant metastases (lung, liver, brain)
Serum marker levels (AFP, β‑hCG, LDH) incorporated into stage

sections.p: Most cases are sporadic, but several risk factors markedly increase incidence, especially in African settings where cryptorchidism and HIV are common.
b: Cryptorchidism (3–5 × risk; persists after orchiopexy)
Family history (father/brother)
Prior contralateral testicular cancer
Infertility, Klinefelter syndrome
HIV infection (immune dysregulation)
In‑utero DES exposure (rare)

sections.p: Patients usually notice a firm, non‑tender nodule. Occasionally, a dull ache, heaviness, or a hydrocele may be reported. Systemic symptoms suggest metastasis.
b: Unilateral painless testicular lump
Scrotal heaviness, occasional dull ache
Gynecomastia (β‑hCG‑producing non‑seminoma)
Weight loss, cough, neurological signs if metastatic

sections.p: Limited resources dictate a stepwise approach: bedside exam → ultrasound → targeted labs. When imaging or markers are unavailable, management relies on clinical stage.

t.b: Confirms solid intratesticular lesion vs hydrocele; assesses size and vascularity
Distinguishes seminoma (AFP normal, β‑hCG may be modestly raised) from non‑seminoma (AFP ↑, β‑hCG ↑)
Screens for pulmonary metastases when CT unavailable
Evaluates retroperitoneal nodes and distant spread

sections.p: Rapid growth, pain, or systemic signs indicate aggressive disease or complications such as torsion, infection, or metastasis.
b: Acute scrotal pain → testicular torsion or infarction
Rapid increase in size → high‑grade tumor
Cough, dyspnea, neurological deficits → lung or brain metastases

sections.p: Primary treatment is radical inguinal orchiectomy. Adjuvant radiotherapy is reserved for seminoma stage I‑II; chemotherapy (BEP) for non‑seminoma or advanced disease. In low‑resource settings, surgery plus simple surveillance may be the only option.
b: Radical inguinal orchiectomy – removes tumor, provides pathology
Seminoma stage I‑II: single‑dose radiotherapy (20 Gy) if available
Non‑seminoma stage II‑III: BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin) – avoid if severe renal or pulmonary disease
Surveillance: regular exam, ultrasound, markers when possible

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects recurrence early. Testicular self‑examination and early orchidopexy for undescended testes reduce risk.
b: Every 3 months for 2 y: exam, ultrasound, markers
Every 6–12 months thereafter up to 5 y
Educate on monthly self‑exam after puberty
Orchiopexy before age 2 lowers cancer risk

sections.p: Several benign scrotal conditions mimic cancer; distinguishing features guide urgent referral.
b: Hydrocele – transilluminates, fluid‑filled on ultrasound
Epididymitis – painful, tender, often with fever; Doppler ↑ flow
Spermatocele – cystic, anechoic, located at epididymal head

sections.p: Tumor markers may be normal in early seminoma; reliance on them alone can delay diagnosis.
b: Normal AFP/β‑hCG does not exclude cancer – always image
LDH can be raised by hemolysis or liver disease
Ultrasound may miss tiny intratesticular lesions; repeat if suspicion persists

whenToSeekHelp: New onset gynecomastia with testicular lump
Cough, neurological symptoms, or unexplained weight loss

faq.q: Can a testicular tumor be felt through the abdomen?
faq.a: No, it is confined to the scrotum; abdominal masses suggest metastatic lymph nodes.

faq.q: Is testicular cancer related to prostate cancer?
faq.a: No, they arise from different cell types and have distinct risk factors.

faq.q: Why is an inguinal approach used for orchiectomy?
faq.a: It avoids scrotal violation, preventing tumor seeding and preserving lymphatic drainage patterns.

exam: A 22‑year‑old presents with a painless left testicular mass; ultrasound unavailable – what is your next step and why? — Perform radical inguinal orchiectomy for both diagnosis and treatment.
How does the presence of elevated β‑hCG change management in a stage I testicular tumor? — Indicates non‑seminoma; requires chemotherapy or closer surveillance rather than radiotherapy alone.
A patient with known seminoma develops gynecomastia; what does this suggest and how should you respond? — β‑hCG production; assess marker levels and consider systemic therapy.

In a low‑resource hospital without CT, how would you stage a suspected metastatic testicular cancer? — Use chest X‑ray for lung spread, abdominal ultrasound for retroperitoneal nodes, and serum markers to approximate stage.
Why is scrotal violation during biopsy contraindicated? — Increases risk of local recurrence and alters lymphatic drainage, complicating later surgery.
What are the key differences between seminoma and non‑seminoma on pathology and treatment? — Seminoma: radiosensitive, normal AFP; non‑seminoma: AFP ↑, requires BEP chemotherapy.

A man with a history of cryptorchidism repaired at age 5 presents with testicular cancer; how does his prior orchiopexy affect prognosis? — Risk remains elevated; earlier orchiopexy reduces but does not eliminate risk, prognosis similar to sporadic cases when treated early.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate imaging for brain metastasis in testicular cancer? — New focal neurological deficit or seizures.
